---
title: "Towers and the places they stand in"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# here() would stop at analysis/, which has its own _quarto.yml. Declaring
# this file's place in the repo fixes the root at the repository itself.
here::i_am("analysis/tower-context.qmd")
source(here::here("scripts", "00_setup.R"))
source(here::here("analysis", "_common.R"))   # data, provisional choices, model
library(cluster)   # silhouette widths; ships with R

# ---- choices this chapter makes, all provisional ---------------------------

# Measures the clustering sees. Logged population at four kernel scales, plus
# tower density at the local and wide scales. Bells are left out because they
# are close to towers x average ring size, and would double-count density.
CLUSTER_VARS <- c("pop_k1km", "pop_k2km", "pop_k4km", "pop_k8km",
                  "towers_k2km", "towers_k8km")

# Number of principal components fed to k-means, and the k shown in detail.
N_PCS      <- 3
K_CLUSTERS <- 6
K_RANGE    <- 3:10

# Bell classes for tables.
BELL_BREAKS <- c(4, 6, 8, 10, Inf)          # 4-5, 6-7, 8-9, 10+
BELL_LABELS <- c("4-5", "6-7", "8-9", "10+")

lg <- function(x) log10(x + 1)     # zeros exist (Lundy); +1 person is harmless
```

```{r}
#| label: load
#| include: false
# Frame towers (D-017, D-019), with their bell class and broad region.
tw <- frame_towers |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    bell_class = cut(.data$bells, BELL_BREAKS, BELL_LABELS, right = FALSE),
    region = dplyr::case_when(
      .data$country %in% c("England", "Wales") ~ "England & Wales",
      .data$country %in% BRITISH_ISLES ~ "Rest of British Isles",
      TRUE ~ .data$country
    )
  )

# Every distance measure the context table carries: kernels first, then
# circles, each from the tightest out. Names are read only by the helpers in
# R/catchment.R.
measures <- grep("^pop_[kr][0-9]+(m|km)$", names(context), value = TRUE) |>
  sub(pattern = "^pop_", replacement = "")
measures <- measures[order(measure_type(measures) != "kernel", measure_metres(measures))]

n_missing_context <- sum(frame$frame_full) -
  sum(frame$frame_full & frame$tower_id %in% context$tower_id)
```

*Prepared by Mark Ainsworth with Claude (Anthropic). Mark set the questions
and made the decisions; Claude drafted the code and text, which Mark
reviewed.*

## Background and brief

**Where this fits.** The census will chase about 1,000 randomly drawn towers
until each one replies. Comparing them with towers that reply unprompted
shows who does not respond, and lets the estimates correct for it. The draw
is to be stratified by number of bells and by what sort of place a tower is
in. Three chapters work towards that:

- this chapter describes the towers and their surroundings;
- *Choosing a classification* turns that description into named place types;
- *Choosing a sampling method* uses the types and measures to design the
  draw.

**Starting points Mark set out.**

- *Urban is not one thing.* At least three effects are mixed together:
  - the size of the settlement, which sets how many people live near enough
    to ring;
  - large towns have fewer towers than their size suggests, because of how
    churches with bells came to be built, except in conurbations made of
    villages that grew together, which have many;
  - city centres, especially the City of London, have towers with almost no
    residents, rung by society bands such as the College Youths and the
    Cumberlands.
- *It should work outside England without rework*, even though the
  dynamics abroad are probably different.
- *Measure around each tower, not by area.* Ready-made area classifications
  are kept for comparison, but are not expected to be the answer.
- *Use distance decay, not just circles.* A circle of fixed radius gives
  full weight just inside its edge and none just outside. A decay kernel
  avoids that cliff. Plain circles are computed too, because they are easier
  to explain.
- *Competition matters as much as distance.* Nearby rival towers shrink a
  catchment, as rival shops do in retail gravity models. People per tower,
  and per bell, stand in for that.
- *Bells matter for parity.* A band much bigger than its ring means people
  sitting out, so people per bell is as relevant as people per tower.
- *Ring size records history.* The number of bells reflects what a place was
  when its bells were cast and augmented: its size, wealth and the standing
  of its church. Mark's own home tower, Amersham, went from 8 to 12 bells
  after he learned there, so the record is not perfect.
- *Villages absorbed into conurbations matter.* Towns grew over villages
  that already had bells, so those towers now sit amid far more people than
  their ring size suggests. Places rarely shrink as much, so the mismatch
  runs mostly one way, and the model should be asymmetric. Mark's analogy is
  used-car adverts: fairly priced cars sell and vanish, overpriced ones
  linger, so a fair valuation model listens most to the cheap side.
- *Tighter scales, and a check for interactions* (Mark, 10 October). Ring
  size correlated best with the tightest measure first computed, the 1 km
  circle. Tighter measures (250 m and 500 m kernels, a 500 m circle) test
  whether that correlation peaks. A decision tree, on the kernels only, looks
  for interactions between scales.

**What this chapter is for.** To show how the measures behave, how they
relate to each other and to ring size, so that the next chapter can draw
boundaries that mean something. Nothing here is a decision.

**Out of scope.** Choosing the place types, and the sampling method.

## What the measures are

Script 08 describes the area around each tower in three ways.

- **Decay kernels**, named `k250m` to `k8km`. Nearer things count more, and
  the weight halves every 250 m, 500 m, 1, 2, 4 or 8 km. The 2 km kernel is
  the main catchment measure. Its scale comes from published travel data for
  weekly voluntary activities, such as swimming and church attendance, which
  imply a half-distance of about 1.5–2.3 km.
- **Plain circles**, named `r500m` to `r10km`. Everything within the radius
  counts equally.
- **Contiguous settlements.** The continuous built-up area the tower stands
  in, traced on the international Degree of Urbanisation's 1 km grid with
  that scheme's own rules, and the number of people living in it. Unlike the
  kernels and circles, this follows the settlement's own edge.

The kernels and circles count three things: **people** (from the EU's Global
Human Settlement Layer), and **towers** and **bells** (from the sampling
frame, the tower itself included). Ratios follow: **people per tower**,
**people per bell**, and **people per km² of land**, which stops the sea
counting as empty country. Columns are named by what they count and how, for
example `pop_k2km` or `density_land_r500m`.

```{r}
#| label: headline
#| include: false
# Computed early so the headline findings below are live numbers.

# Kernels against circles
pop_mat <- tw |> dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(paste0("pop_", measures)))
rho  <- stats::cor(pop_mat, method = "spearman")
kern <- paste0("pop_", measures[measure_type(measures) == "kernel"])
rad  <- paste0("pop_", measures[measure_type(measures) == "radius"])
best_radius <- tibble::tibble(kernel = kern) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    best_radius = rad[apply(rho[kern, rad, drop = FALSE], 1, which.max)],
    spearman    = round(apply(rho[kern, rad, drop = FALSE], 1, max), 3)
  )
k2 <- dplyr::filter(best_radius, .data$kernel == "pop_k2km")

# Ring size against density at every scale, ordered by how far each measure
# really looks (the radius holding half its weight).
scale_cor <- tibble::tibble(column = grep("^density_land_", names(bi), value = TRUE)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    measure   = sub("^density_land_", "", .data$column),
    label     = measure_label(.data$measure),
    type      = measure_type(.data$measure),
    half_mass = measure_half_mass_m(.data$measure),
    spearman  = purrr::map_dbl(.data$column, \(v)
      stats::cor(bi$bells, bi[[v]], method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"))
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$half_mass)
best_scale <- dplyr::slice_max(scale_cor, .data$spearman, n = 1)
tightest   <- dplyr::slice_min(scale_cor, .data$half_mass, n = 1)
peaks <- tightest$spearman < best_scale$spearman

# Contiguous settlements
in_centre_share <- mean(!is.na(tw$centre_pop))
big_cluster     <- mean(tw$urban_pop >= 5e6, na.rm = TRUE)

# Principal components
X <- tw |>
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(CLUSTER_VARS)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(), lg)) |>
  scale()
pca <- stats::prcomp(X)
scores <- as.data.frame(pca$x[, 1:N_PCS])
var_share <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
pc1_all_same_sign <- length(unique(sign(pca$rotation[, 1]))) == 1
pc2_top <- names(sort(abs(pca$rotation[, 2]), decreasing = TRUE))[1:2]
# Plain-English names for the findings text
plain <- function(v) {
  what <- dplyr::case_when(startsWith(v, "pop_")    ~ "population",
                           startsWith(v, "towers_") ~ "tower density",
                           startsWith(v, "bells_")  ~ "bell density",
                           TRUE ~ v)
  paste0(what, " (", measure_label(v), ")")
}

# Clusters and silhouettes
km_fits <- purrr::map(K_RANGE, \(k) stats::kmeans(scores, centers = k, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100))
sil_idx <- sample(nrow(scores), min(2500, nrow(scores)))
d_sub   <- stats::dist(scores[sil_idx, ])
sil_by_k <- purrr::map_dbl(km_fits, \(f)
  mean(cluster::silhouette(f$cluster[sil_idx], d_sub)[, "sil_width"]))
k_best <- K_RANGE[which.max(sil_by_k)]

london_top <- bi |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$in_frame) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(.data$u, n = 50) |>
  dplyr::summarise(share = mean(grepl("London", .data$display))) |>
  dplyr::pull(.data$share)
```

## Headline findings

- **Ring size tracks the settlement's core, at a scale of about
  `r fmt(best_scale$half_mass)` m.** Its rank correlation with density is
  highest for the `r best_scale$label` (`r round(best_scale$spearman, 3)`).
  `r if (peaks) paste0("It is slightly lower for the tighter ", tightest$label, " (", round(tightest$spearman, 3), "), so the curve peaks, gently, rather than rising without limit.") else paste0("It is still rising at the tightest measure, the ", tightest$label, ", so the peak may be tighter still.")`
- **Rings of 3 to 7 bells sit in the same kind of place.** Allowing for
  growth since their bells were hung, the typical density around a ring of 3
  is `r fmt(frontier$frontier[1])` people per km² of land, and around a ring
  of 6–7 it is `r fmt(frontier$frontier[3])`. The step comes with rings of 8
  (`r fmt(frontier$frontier[4])`) and 10 or more (`r fmt(frontier$frontier[5])`).
- **Growth around towers is large and one-sided.** In the asymmetric model,
  "growth since the bells" varies more than ordinary noise
  (`r round(sfa$su, 2)` against `r round(sfa$sv, 2)` on a log10 scale). Of
  the 50 towers grown around most, `r pct(london_top)` are in London.
- **Contiguity separates places that distance cannot.**
  `r pct(in_centre_share)` of frame towers stand inside an urban centre, a
  continuous built-up area of 50,000 people or more. The looser "urban
  cluster" joins too much: `r pct(big_cluster)` of the frame towers that are
  in one are in a cluster of more than five million people.
- **The towers do not fall into natural groups.** The best silhouette score
  is `r round(max(sil_by_k), 2)`, at k = `r k_best`.
  `r if (max(sil_by_k) < 0.5) "That is below the 0.5 usually taken as clear structure, so any classes are a convenience for communication, not a discovery." else "That is above the 0.5 usually taken as clear structure, so the groups may be real."`
- **The circles track the kernels closely.** The 2 km kernel ranks towers
  almost exactly as the `r measure_label(k2$best_radius)` does (rank
  correlation `r k2$spearman`).

## How each measure is distributed

Each panel is one measure on a log scale. The kernels and circles should look
alike in shape; the question is how much they differ in spread.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dist
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of each measure across frame towers (log10 of value + 1)."
long <- tw |>
  dplyr::select("tower_id", dplyr::matches(paste0("^(pop|towers|pop_per_bell)_(",
                                                 paste(measures, collapse = "|"), ")$"))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-"tower_id", names_to = c("family", "measure"),
                      names_pattern = "^(pop_per_bell|pop|towers)_(.*)$") |>
  dplyr::mutate(measure = factor(.data$measure, levels = measures),
                family  = factor(.data$family, levels = c("pop", "towers", "pop_per_bell"),
                                 labels = c("Population", "Frame towers", "Population per bell")))

ggplot(long, aes(lg(value))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = PAL_CAT[1], colour = NA) +
  facet_grid(measure ~ family, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "log10(value + 1)", y = "Towers") +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-quantiles
long |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    p05 = stats::quantile(.data$value, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    p25 = stats::quantile(.data$value, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    p50 = stats::quantile(.data$value, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE),
    p75 = stats::quantile(.data$value, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    p95 = stats::quantile(.data$value, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c("family", "measure")
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$family, .data$measure) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(p05:p95, \(x) signif(x, 3))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Quantiles across frame towers")
```

## Do the circles add anything to the kernels?

If a circle ranks towers almost exactly as a kernel does, the circle can be
used to explain the kernel to a meeting, and nothing is lost. The table gives,
for each kernel, the circle with the highest rank correlation.

Expect the matching circle to be much wider than the half-distance. Over
uniform ground, half of a kernel's total weight lies within about 2.4
half-distances, and 90% within about 5.6. So a "1 km" kernel draws most of its
weight from within about 5 km. To a meeting, describe the 2 km kernel as
"people within about 5 km, nearer ones counting more", not as "people within
2 km".

```{r}
#| label: tbl-kernel-radius
best_radius |>
  dplyr::mutate(kernel = measure_label(.data$kernel),
                best_radius = measure_label(.data$best_radius)) |>
  dplyr::rename(`best-matching circle` = "best_radius") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-kernel-radius
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "2 km kernel against the 2 km and 5 km circles. Points far off the band are towers where the circle's edge cuts through a town."
tw |>
  dplyr::select("pop_k2km", "pop_r2km", "pop_r5km") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c("pop_r2km", "pop_r5km"), names_to = "radius") |>
  ggplot(aes(lg(pop_k2km), lg(value))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.25, colour = PAL_CAT[1]) +
  facet_wrap(~radius) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(lg(stats::quantile(tw$pop_k2km, 0.002)), NA)) +
  labs(x = "log10 population, 2 km kernel", y = "log10 population, circle")
```

## Correlation structure

Rank correlations across every measure, clustered so that measures that move
together sit together. Large blocks of near-1 mean redundant measures; the
interesting structure is in the off-diagonal blocks.

```{r}
#| label: fig-corr
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "Spearman correlations between all measures."
all_vars <- tw |>
  dplyr::select(dplyr::matches(paste0("^(pop|towers|bells|pop_per_bell)_(",
                                      paste(measures, collapse = "|"), ")$")))
cm <- stats::cor(all_vars, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
ord <- stats::hclust(stats::as.dist(1 - cm))$order
cm_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cm)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Var1 = factor(.data$Var1, levels = colnames(cm)[ord]),
                Var2 = factor(.data$Var2, levels = colnames(cm)[ord]))

ggplot(cm_long, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#eb6834", mid = "#f2f2f2", high = "#184f95",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Spearman") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
```

A handful of towers have close to zero population within the 2 km kernel.
They are listed here, then kept out of the axis ranges below so they do not

#| label: tbl-empty
tw |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$pop_k2km < 50) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$pop_k2km) |>
  dplyr::transmute(.data$display, .data$country, pop_k2km = round(.data$pop_k2km),
                   pop_k8km = fmt(.data$pop_k8km), .data$special) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Frame towers with fewer than 50 people in the 2 km kernel")

# Axis floor for the scatter plots: the 0.2nd percentile of the 2 km kernel.

floor_8km <- lg(stats::quantile(tw$pop_k8km, 0.002))

## Local scale against wider scale

This plane carries most of the three effects Mark described:

- **Up the diagonal:** hamlet, then village, then town, then city.
- **Above the diagonal:** low local population but high wider population. A
  village on the edge of a conurbation, or a tower in a merged-villages
  suburb.
- **Below the diagonal:** a free-standing town with empty country around it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-local-wide
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Local (2 km kernel) against wider (8 km kernel) population, coloured by the international Degree of Urbanisation."
ggplot(tw, aes(lg(pop_k2km), lg(pop_k8km), colour = smod_class)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = PAL_SMOD, drop = TRUE, name = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1), nrow = 2)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(floor_2km, NA), ylim = c(floor_8km, NA)) +
  labs(x = "log10 population, 2 km kernel", y = "log10 population, 8 km kernel")
```

The vertical distance from the main band is a candidate single index of
"embeddedness": how much bigger the wider area is than the place itself.

```{r}
#| label: fig-embedded
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Embeddedness, log10(8 km) minus log10(2 km), by Degree of Urbanisation."
tw |>
  dplyr::mutate(embedded = lg(.data$pop_k8km) - lg(.data$pop_k2km)) |>
  ggplot(aes(smod_class, embedded)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.4, fill = "#cde2fb", colour = "#184f95") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log10(8 km) - log10(2 km)")
```

## Competition: people per tower and per bell

City centres should stand out as many towers and few residents. Dense
conurbations should show more towers than their population alone predicts.

## Contiguous settlements: following the settlement's own edge

**Why they are needed.** Kernels and circles count everyone within reach,
whether or not they live in the same place as the tower. A free-standing city
ringed by green belt and a stretch of continuous suburb can therefore score
alike. What tells them apart is whether the built-up area is continuous.

**How they are traced.** The international Degree of Urbanisation already
labels every 1 km cell. Script 08 joins the labelled cells back into
continuous patches, using the scheme's own rules, and sums each patch's
population.^[Eurostat (2021), *Applying the Degree of Urbanisation*. See
*Methods and sources*.]

- **Urban centre:** cells of at least 1,500 people per km², joined edge to
  edge only, "without diagonals", and totalling at least 50,000 people.
- **Urban cluster:** cells of at least 300 per km², joined "including
  diagonals", totalling at least 5,000. Centres are included.
- **Rural cluster:** the grid's nearest thing to a village, from 500 to
  4,999 people.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-contiguous
tw |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$british_isles) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    where = dplyr::case_when(
      !is.na(.data$centre_pop) & .data$centre_pop >= 1e6 ~ "Urban centre of 1 million or more",
      !is.na(.data$centre_pop) & .data$centre_pop >= 2e5 ~ "Urban centre of 200,000 to 1 million",
      !is.na(.data$centre_pop)                         ~ "Urban centre of 50,000 to 200,000",
      !is.na(.data$urban_pop)                          ~ "Urban cluster, outside any centre",
      !is.na(.data$rural_cluster_pop)                  ~ "Rural cluster",
      TRUE                                             ~ "None: dispersed rural"
    ),
    where = factor(.data$where, levels = c(
      "Urban centre of 1 million or more", "Urban centre of 200,000 to 1 million",
      "Urban centre of 50,000 to 200,000", "Urban cluster, outside any centre",
      "Rural cluster", "None: dispersed rural"))
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(towers = dplyr::n(),
                   `median people within 1 km` = fmt(stats::median(.data$pop_r1km)),
                   `rings of 8 or more` = pct(mean(.data$bells >= 8)),
                   .by = "where") |>
  dplyr::mutate(share = pct(.data$towers / sum(.data$towers))) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$where) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "British Isles frame towers by the contiguous settlement they stand in")
```

**Urban centres work; urban clusters join too much.** Because urban clusters
join diagonally and include low-density suburban cells, they chain towns
together. In the South East of England, one cluster runs from London out to
places such as St Albans and Welwyn. Urban centres, joined edge to edge at a
higher density, keep St Albans separate from London while placing Staines
inside it. That matches how the places feel to ringers who know them (the
next chapter's sense check has the detail).

`r sum(tw$settlement_window_edge)` frame towers sit in a settlement that was
cut by its tracing window, almost all of them in or near London. For them the
settlement's population is a lower bound, but still in the millions, so no
class changes.

## Ring size is a record of what a place used to be

The question: does the number of bells tell us what sort of place a tower
is in? The figure shows today's density around every British Isles tower,
grouped by ring size.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ring-density
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "People per km² of land within the 2 km kernel, by ring size (British Isles, all ringable full-circle rings of 3+). Boxes: middle half. Black diamonds: the asymmetric model's typical density for each ring size, with 95% intervals."
ggplot(bi, aes(ring_class, .data[[DENSITY_VAR]])) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = ring_class), outlier.size = 0.3, outlier.alpha = 0.3,
               colour = "grey30", width = 0.6) +
  geom_pointrange(data = frontier, aes(y = frontier, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
                  shape = 23, fill = "black", size = 0.4) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = RING_PAL, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Bells in the ring", y = "People per km² of land (log scale)")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ring-density
bi |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    towers = dplyr::n(),
    `10th pct` = stats::quantile(.data[[DENSITY_VAR]], 0.10),
    `25th`     = stats::quantile(.data[[DENSITY_VAR]], 0.25),
    median     = stats::median(.data[[DENSITY_VAR]]),
    `75th`     = stats::quantile(.data[[DENSITY_VAR]], 0.75),
    `90th`     = stats::quantile(.data[[DENSITY_VAR]], 0.90),
    .by = "ring_class"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$ring_class) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-c("ring_class", "towers"), fmt)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "People per km² of land around towers, by ring size")
```

Two things stand out. The spread within every ring size is enormous: the
middle half of towers with six bells spans more than a factor of four in
density. And the spread is lopsided. Each box has a long upper tail of towers
in far denser places than is typical for their ring size.

### Which distance scale tracks ring size best?

Kernels and circles of the same nominal size look very different distances.
To compare them on one scale, each is placed by the radius that holds half
its weight: about 2.4 half-distances for a kernel, and 0.71 of the radius for
a circle.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scale
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Rank correlation of ring size with land density, against how far each measure really looks (radius holding half its weight, log scale). British Isles, rings of 3+."
ggplot(scale_cor, aes(half_mass, spearman, colour = type)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = type), linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(aes(label = .data$measure), vjust = -0.9, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.15))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(kernel = PAL_CAT[1], radius = PAL_CAT[2]),
                      labels = c(kernel = "Kernel", radius = "Circle"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Radius holding half the weight (m)", y = "Spearman correlation with bells")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scale
scale_cor |>
  dplyr::transmute(measure = .data$label,
                   `half its weight within (m)` = fmt(.data$half_mass),
                   spearman = round(.data$spearman, 3)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Rank correlation of ring size with land density, tightest measure first")
```

**What the scales show.** The correlation is highest for the
`r best_scale$label`, which holds half its weight within about
`r fmt(best_scale$half_mass)` m.
`r if (peaks) paste0("It is lower again for the tightest measure, the ", tightest$label, ", so the correlation peaks rather than rising without limit. The peak is gentle: every measure reaching between about ", fmt(min(scale_cor$half_mass[scale_cor$spearman >= best_scale$spearman - 0.03])), " and ", fmt(max(scale_cor$half_mass[scale_cor$spearman >= best_scale$spearman - 0.03])), " m scores within 0.03 of the best.") else paste0("It is still rising at the tightest measure, the ", tightest$label, ", so the peak may be tighter still.")`
Placed by their real reach, kernels and circles agree at the scale of the
core. At wider scales the kernels track ring size slightly better than
circles of the same reach, as expected of a measure without a hard edge.

**Why the core.** Churches stand at the historic core of their settlement,
and ring size reflects the size and standing of that core. Measures tighter
than the core pick up the churchyard and the next street. Wider measures
dilute the core with countryside or neighbouring places. The peak marks the
natural size of a settlement core, as ring size sees it.

**What it does not mean.** It does not make the tightest scale the right one
for every purpose. Recruitment depends on the wider catchment, which ring
size does not measure. Choosing a scale because it tracks ring size best
would also bring ring size back into the place measures by another route.

### Decision trees: what separates 8, 10 and 12 bells

A classification tree (CART)^[Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone (1984). See
*Methods and sources*.] splits the towers again and again on whichever
measure best separates large rings from smaller ones. It finds thresholds
and interactions on its own: for example, whether a dense core matters more
when the area around it is sparse.

**Why three trees.** One tree each separates rings of 8 or more, 10 or more,
and 12 or more from the rest. If the drivers differ, that says something
about what each size of ring belonged to. One idea worth testing (Mark, 11
October): bells were historically about earshot. Heavier rings carry
further, so if earshot shaped where large rings were hung, the trees for 10
and 12 should lean on *wider* kernels than the tree for 8. If instead large
rings belong to the size and wealth of a settlement's core, all three should
lean on the tight kernels.

**Choices that keep them honest and comparable.**

- **Kernels only.** Kernels and circles of similar reach are nearly
  interchangeable. Offering both lets a tree pick between near-twins, which
  spreads the importance between them and makes it hard to read (Mark, 10
  October). The coast is the one other measure offered, because it is not a
  distance measure. Isolation is left out: it is a ratio of two scales, and
  finding how scales combine is the tree's job.
- **Equal weight to both sides.** Rings of 12 are rare, so a tree left to
  itself would mostly learn to say "not 12". Each tree is told to treat the
  two classes as equally common (equal priors), so all three are judged on
  the same footing. The group tables still show the raw shares.
- **The same settings for all three.** The smallest group allowed is 30
  towers, and each tree is pruned back to the simplest one whose
  cross-validated error is within one standard error of the best (the usual
  "one-SE rule"), so a tree for a rare class cannot chase noise.
- **Credit only for the splits actually used.** A tree can also credit
  measures that would have made nearly as good a split ("surrogates").
  Near-twin kernels then share the credit, which blurs the question of
  scale, so surrogates are switched off.
- **A diagnostic only.** The target is ring size, so using the splits as
  classes would build ring size back into the classification.

```{r}
#| label: trees
tree_base <- bi |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$in_frame) |>
  dplyr::select("bells", dplyr::matches("^density_land_k[0-9]+(m|km)$"), "coast") |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("density_land_"), \(x) log10(x))) |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::if_all(dplyr::everything(), is.finite))
tree_label <- \(v) ifelse(grepl("^density_land_", v),
                          measure_label(ifelse(grepl("^density_land_", v), v, "k1km")), v)
reach_of <- \(v) ifelse(grepl("^density_land_", v),
                        measure_half_mass_m(ifelse(grepl("^density_land_", v), v, "k1km")), NA)

fit_tree <- function(k) {
  d <- tree_base |>
    dplyr::mutate(target = factor(.data$bells >= k, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                                  labels = c(paste("under", k), paste(k, "or more")))) |>
    dplyr::select(-"bells")
  set.seed(2026)  # the cross-validation folds are random
  tr <- rpart::rpart(target ~ ., data = d, method = "class",
                     parms = list(prior = c(0.5, 0.5)),
                     control = rpart::rpart.control(cp = 0.002, minbucket = 30,
                                                    maxsurrogate = 0))
  # Prune by the one-standard-error rule: the smallest tree whose
  # cross-validated error is within one standard error of the best.
  ct <- tr$cptable
  best <- which.min(ct[, "xerror"])
  ok <- which(ct[, "xerror"] <= ct[best, "xerror"] + ct[best, "xstd"])[1]
  tr <- rpart::prune(tr, cp = ct[ok, "CP"] * 1.0001)
  imp <- tr$variable.importance / sum(tr$variable.importance)
  cp  <- as.data.frame(tr$cptable)
  first <- tr$frame$var[1]
  list(k = k, tree = tr, leaves = leaf_rules(tr), importance = imp,
       positives = sum(d$target == levels(d$target)[2]),
       first = first,
       first_at = 10^tr$splits[first, "index"],
       splits = max(cp$nsplit),
       cv_gain = 1 - min(cp$xerror),
       # Importance-weighted reach: where, on average, the tree looks.
       reach = sum(imp[grepl("^density_land_", names(imp))] *
                     reach_of(names(imp)[grepl("^density_land_", names(imp))])) /
               sum(imp[grepl("^density_land_", names(imp))]))
}
trees <- purrr::map(c(8, 10, 12), fit_tree)
names(trees) <- paste0(c(8, 10, 12), "+")

tibble::tibble(
  target = paste(names(trees), "bells"),
  `towers in that class` = purrr::map_int(trees, "positives"),
  `first split` = purrr::map_chr(trees, \(t) paste0(tree_label(t$first), " at ", fmt(t$first_at))),
  splits = purrr::map_dbl(trees, "splits"),
  `its reach (m)` = fmt(purrr::map_dbl(trees, \(t) reach_of(t$first))),
  `error cut on cross-validation` = pct(purrr::map_dbl(trees, "cv_gain"))
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Three trees compared (first split in people per km² of land)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-tree-reach
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Rank correlation between being in each ring-size class and land density, against each kernel's reach (radius holding half its weight). British Isles frame towers."
reach_cor <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  k = c(8, 10, 12),
  column = grep("^density_land_k[0-9]+(m|km)$", names(tree_base), value = TRUE)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    reach = measure_half_mass_m(.data$column),
    spearman = purrr::map2_dbl(.data$k, .data$column, \(k, v)
      stats::cor(as.numeric(tree_base$bells >= k), tree_base[[v]], method = "spearman")),
    class = factor(paste0(.data$k, "+ bells"), levels = paste0(c(8, 10, 12), "+ bells"))
  )
reach_peak <- reach_cor |> dplyr::slice_max(.data$spearman, n = 1, by = "class")
ggplot(reach_cor, aes(reach, spearman, colour = class)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = stats::setNames(PAL_CAT[1:3], levels(reach_cor$class)), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Radius holding half the kernel's weight (m)", y = "Spearman correlation")
```

**Where each tree looks.** Pruned to what cross-validation supports, each
tree keeps `r if (all(purrr::map_dbl(trees, "splits") == 1)) "a single split" else "only a few splits"`.
The tree for 8 or more splits on the `r tree_label(trees[["8+"]]$first)` at
`r fmt(trees[["8+"]]$first_at)` people per km² of land; for 10 or more, on
the `r tree_label(trees[["10+"]]$first)` at `r fmt(trees[["10+"]]$first_at)`;
for 12 or more, on the `r tree_label(trees[["12+"]]$first)` at
`r fmt(trees[["12+"]]$first_at)`. The simple correlations in the figure peak
at `r paste0(fmt(reach_peak$reach), " m for ", reach_peak$class, collapse = "; ")`.
`r ties <- reach_cor |> dplyr::group_by(.data$class) |> dplyr::summarise(flat = sum(.data$spearman >= max(.data$spearman) - 0.005), kept = .data$spearman[.data$column == "density_land_k2km"] / max(.data$spearman)); paste0("But the peaks are shallow: for ", paste(ties$class[ties$flat > 1], collapse = " and "), " the two tightest kernels score within 0.005 of each other, so a peak's position is not a reliable signal. The decay is more telling. At the 2 km kernel, the correlation keeps ", paste0(pct(ties$kept), " of its peak for ", ties$class, collapse = ", "), ". ", if (ties$kept[3] > ties$kept[1] + 0.05) "Larger rings hold their link with density further out, which is what the earshot idea predicts, though only mildly." else "Larger rings do not hold their link with density further out, which counts against earshot as the main story.")`
The density at the split also rises with ring size: larger rings need a
denser core, as well as perhaps a wider one.

**The strongest case against reading this as earshot.** First, the step is
small: one notch on a grid of six kernels, each double the last, resting on
`r trees[["12+"]]$positives` towers. Second, rings of 12 stand
mostly in cities, and a city's core is wider than a village's. So a scale
that widens for larger rings may mean only that larger rings sit in larger
places, whatever their sound carried. Separating the two needs a comparison
*within* one ring size: among rings of 8, do the heavier ones belong to a
wider area? Tenor weight is in Dove, but not yet in the frame.

The trees for larger rings rest on fewer towers, so their splits are less
stable: read their groups as suggestions.

**The groups each tree finds.** Shares are the raw share of towers in the
class, not adjusted for the equal weighting.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tree-leaves
#| results: asis
for (nm in names(trees)) {
  t <- trees[[nm]]
  print(knitr::kable(
    t$leaves |> dplyr::transmute(`towers in the group` = .data$rule, towers = .data$towers,
                                 share = pct(.data$share)) |>
      dplyr::rename(!!paste("rings of", sub("\\+", " or more", nm)) := "share"),
    caption = paste0("Tree for ", sub("\\+", " or more", nm), " bells: its groups, fewest first (people per km² of land)")))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tree-interaction
#| include: false
# Look for the typical interaction in the 8+ tree: two groups sharing a range
# on one measure and split on a second, wider one.
leaves <- trees[["8+"]]$leaves
pair <- leaves |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl(";", .data$rule)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(core = sub(";.*$", "", .data$rule),
                wider = sub("^[^;]*; ", "", .data$rule))
interaction <- nrow(pair) == 2 && dplyr::n_distinct(pair$core) == 1 &&
  !grepl(";", pair$wider[1]) && !grepl(";", pair$wider[2])
if (interaction) {
  sparse <- dplyr::filter(pair, grepl("under", .data$wider))
  dense  <- dplyr::filter(pair, !grepl("under", .data$wider))
  interaction <- nrow(sparse) == 1 && nrow(dense) == 1
}
say <- \(x) sub("(kernel|circle) ", "\\1 is ", x)   # "1 km kernel under 420" -> "... is under 420"
```

`r if (interaction) paste0("**The tree for 8 or more finds an interaction.** Among towers where the ", say(pair$core[1]), " people per km² of land, those where the ", say(sparse$wider), " have ", pct(sparse$share), " rings of 8 or more, against ", pct(dense$share), " where the ", say(dense$wider), ". ", if (sparse$share > dense$share) "The same core density means more where the surroundings are sparse. That is the free-standing market town against the village absorbed into a larger place: alike at the church, different in history. A place classification that separates the two, without using bells, is on the right lines." else "Here denser surroundings go with larger rings.") else "**No interaction between scales survives pruning.** An unpruned tree for 8 or more does split again on wider kernels, suggesting that a moderately dense core means more where its surroundings are sparse, the free-standing market town against the absorbed village. But cross-validation does not support those extra splits, so treat that pattern as a hint, not a finding."`

**The better use of trees comes after fieldwork.** Once the census measures
band size and response for the chased towers, a model-based tree^[Hothorn,
Hornik & Zeileis (2006); Zeileis, Hothorn & Hornik (2008).] can partition the
towers by how those outcomes vary with the place measures. That would give
classes tuned to what the census is actually about, with no circularity.

## A one-sided model separates the bells' story from later growth

**Why an ordinary model misleads.** A standard ordinal regression of ring
size on density^[McCullagh (1980). See *Methods and sources*.] assumes the
scatter around the line is symmetric. Here it is not. A village swallowed by
London has a density hundreds of times what its six bells suggest, and no
plausible process produces the mirror image. Fitting a symmetric model lets
those swallowed villages drag every boundary upwards.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-polr
po <- MASS::polr(ring_class ~ ld, data = bi, Hess = TRUE)
tibble::tibble(
  boundary = names(po$zeta),
  `density at boundary (people per km² of land)` = fmt(10^(po$zeta / stats::coef(po)))
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Boundaries from a symmetric ordinal model, for comparison")
```

Where the boundaries above run from single figures to tens of thousands of
people per km², the symmetric model cannot be describing real places.

**The asymmetric model.** Mark's used-car analogy has an established
statistical counterpart: the *stochastic frontier* model, developed in
economics to separate a firm's random luck from its persistent
inefficiency.^[Aigner, Lovell & Schmidt (1977); Meeusen & van den Broeck
(1977).] The model splits each tower's density into three parts:

- **What its ring size implies**, one value per ring-size class.
- **Ordinary noise**, which can go either way: local accidents of geography
  and history.
- **Growth since**, which can only push density up: the town that grew
  around the village.

The model estimates how big each part is from the shape of the data alone,
without being told which towers were absorbed. The ring-size values it
returns are the densities typical of each ring size before growth: the black
diamonds in the ring-size figure.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sfa
frontier |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c("frontier", "lower", "upper"), fmt)) |>
  dplyr::rename(`ring size` = "ring_class",
                `typical density before growth` = "frontier",
                `95% lower` = "lower", `95% upper` = "upper") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Asymmetric model: typical density by ring size (people per km² of land, 2 km kernel)")
```

The spread of "growth since" (`r round(sfa$su, 2)`) is larger than the
spread of ordinary noise (`r round(sfa$sv, 2)`), both in log10 units. In
plain terms, growth explains more of the differences between towers with the
same ring size than chance does. `r if (!sfa$converged) "**The fit did not converge cleanly: treat these numbers with caution.**" else ""`

For each tower, the model also estimates how much of its density is "growth
since", using the Jondrow method.^[Jondrow, Lovell, Materov & Schmidt
(1982).] That estimate is called `u` below, in log10 units: a `u` of 1 means
the tower's surroundings are about ten times as dense as its ring size
alone would suggest.

### Is "growth since" picking up absorbed villages?

If it is, towers with high `u` should sit among many other towers, because
every swallowed village brought its own church.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-u-checks
bi |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    towers = dplyr::n(),
    `median u` = round(stats::median(.data$u), 2),
    `median towers nearby (2 km kernel)` = round(stats::median(.data$towers_k2km), 1),
    .by = "smod_class"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$`median u`) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Growth since the bells, by international Degree of Urbanisation class")
```

The rank correlation between `u` and the number of towers nearby is
`r round(stats::cor(bi$u, bi$towers_k2km, method = "spearman"), 2)`.

The towers grown around most, and the towers with the most bells for their
surroundings, are the ones ringers will recognise most easily:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-u-extremes
bind <- function(d, label) d |> dplyr::transmute(group = label, .data$display,
  `people per km²` = fmt(.data[[DENSITY_VAR]]), u = round(.data$u, 2))
dplyr::bind_rows(
  bi |> dplyr::filter(.data$in_frame) |>
    dplyr::slice_max(.data$u, n = 12) |> bind("Most grown around"),
  bi |> dplyr::filter(.data$in_frame) |>
    dplyr::slice_min(.data$resid, n = 12) |> bind("Most bells for the place")
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The second list mixes the historically important but now quiet (Dales and
Welsh Marches churches) with modern exceptions such as ringing centres and
Lundy. The model cannot tell those apart, and nor should it: both are towers
whose ring size does not reflect today's population.

## Isolation and the coast

**Isolation** compares a tower's local density with its wider area: log10
of land density in the 1 km circle divided by land density in the 8 km
kernel. Above zero means a place denser than its surroundings, such as a
market town in open country. Below zero means a sparse spot in a dense
region, such as a village in a city's orbit.

**Coast** is the share of the 8 km kernel's weight that falls on sea.
Because density is measured per km² of land, the sea no longer makes a
coastal town look empty. The coast is kept as its own measure, because the
sea still halves the pool of people who can reach the tower.

```{r}
#| label: fig-isolation
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Isolation against coast, frame towers, coloured by the international Degree of Urbanisation."
ggplot(tw, aes(coast, isolation, colour = smod_class)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = PAL_SMOD, name = NULL, drop = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1), nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Share of the 8 km kernel that is sea",
       y = "Isolation: log10(local / wider land density)")
```

## Do the towers fall into natural groups?

If the towers formed clear groups, the classification could simply name
them. Principal components boil six measures (logged and standardised) down
to a few combined scores, and k-means looks for groups in those scores.

```{r}
#| label: pca
tibble::tibble(
  component = paste0("PC", seq_along(pca$sdev)),
  variance  = scales::percent(pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2), 0.1),
  cumulative = scales::percent(cumsum(pca$sdev^2) / sum(pca$sdev^2), 0.1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Variance explained")

round(pca$rotation[, 1:min(4, ncol(X))], 2) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Loadings")
```

**Two dimensions carry `r pct(sum(var_share[1:2]))` of the variation.**
`r if (pc1_all_same_sign) "The first moves with every measure at once, so it is overall size." else "The first does not move with every measure, so read its loadings before calling it size."`
The second is driven mostly by `r plain(pc2_top[1])` and
`r plain(pc2_top[2])`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Towers on the first two components, coloured by Degree of Urbanisation."
ggplot(dplyr::bind_cols(tw, scores), aes(PC1, PC2, colour = smod_class)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = PAL_SMOD, drop = TRUE, name = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1), nrow = 2))
```

k-means on the first `r N_PCS` components, for k from `r min(K_RANGE)` to
`r max(K_RANGE)`. The silhouette width measures how cleanly a clustering
separates the data, from −1 to 1; 0.5 or more is usually taken as clear
structure.

```{r}
#| label: fig-k
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Within-cluster sum of squares and mean silhouette width by k (silhouette on a random 2,500 towers)."
k_diag <- tibble::tibble(
  k = K_RANGE,
  within_ss = purrr::map_dbl(km_fits, "tot.withinss"),
  silhouette = sil_by_k
) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-"k") |>
  dplyr::mutate(name = dplyr::recode(.data$name,
    within_ss = "Total within-cluster sum of squares",
    silhouette = "Mean silhouette width"))

ggplot(k_diag, aes(k, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL_CAT[1], linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL_CAT[1], size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = K_RANGE) +
  labs(y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: clusters
fit <- km_fits[[which(K_RANGE == K_CLUSTERS)]]

# Label clusters in a stable order (by median wider population, then local),
# so C1 is always the most rural.
tw$cluster_raw <- fit$cluster
cl_order <- tw |>
  dplyr::summarise(w = stats::median(.data$pop_k8km), l = stats::median(.data$pop_k2km),
                   .by = "cluster_raw") |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$w, .data$l) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cluster = factor(paste0("C", dplyr::row_number()),
                                 levels = paste0("C", seq_len(K_CLUSTERS))))
tw <- tw |>
  dplyr::left_join(cl_order |> dplyr::select("cluster_raw", "cluster"), by = "cluster_raw")
PAL_CL <- stats::setNames(PAL_CAT[seq_len(K_CLUSTERS)], levels(tw$cluster))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cluster-profile
modal <- \(x) names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
tw |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    towers        = dplyr::n(),
    share         = scales::percent(dplyr::n() / nrow(tw), 0.1),
    pop_2km       = fmt(stats::median(.data$pop_k2km)),
    pop_8km       = fmt(stats::median(.data$pop_k8km)),
    towers_2km    = round(stats::median(.data$towers_k2km), 1),
    pop_per_bell_2km = fmt(stats::median(.data$pop_per_bell_k2km)),
    modal_smod    = modal(.data$smod_class),
    median_bells  = stats::median(.data$bells),
    .by = "cluster"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$cluster) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0("Cluster profiles at k = ", K_CLUSTERS, " (medians)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cluster-plane
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Clusters on the local-against-wider plane."
ggplot(tw, aes(lg(pop_k2km), lg(pop_k8km), colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = PAL_CL, name = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1), nrow = 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(floor_2km, NA), ylim = c(floor_8km, NA)) +
  labs(x = "log10 population, 2 km kernel", y = "log10 population, 8 km kernel")
```

**What the clusters say.** With a best silhouette of
`r round(max(sil_by_k), 2)`, the clusters cut a continuum rather than
finding groups. The plane above shows it: the clusters are slices of one
cloud. Settlement is a continuum, so any classes must be chosen for meaning
and communication, which is the next chapter's job.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-special
tw |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data$special)) |>
  dplyr::count(.data$special, .data$cluster) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "cluster", values_from = "n", values_fill = 0, names_sort = TRUE) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Draft special-case list against clusters")
```

The City of London towers do not form a cluster of their own. That supports
handling them by list rather than by measure.

## Outside the British Isles

The measures use the same definitions everywhere. Whether they mean the same
thing abroad is a separate question.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-abroad
tw |>
  dplyr::count(.data$region, .data$smod_class) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "smod_class", values_from = "n", values_fill = 0, names_sort = TRUE) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Frame towers by region and Degree of Urbanisation")
```

## For the analytical team

Questions this chapter is meant to help answer:

1. **Which scale describes a tower's own place?** The ring-size peak points
   to a core of about `r fmt(best_scale$half_mass)` m. Is that the right
   scale for "own settlement", or should it be chosen on other grounds?
2. **Kernels or circles?** At the core scale they agree once placed by their
   real reach. Use whichever is easier to explain there; prefer kernels for
   wide catchments.
3. **Is "growth since the bells" worth keeping** as a measure of absorbed
   villages, alongside the contiguous-settlement measures?
4. **Do the special-case towers need a list?** The clusters suggest so.

## Methods and sources

**Central place theory.** Christaller, W. (1933), *Die zentralen Orte in
Süddeutschland*, Jena: Gustav Fischer. Settlements form a hierarchy in which
larger places serve wider areas and hold more specialised functions. A
church's ring size is plausibly one such function.

**Contiguous settlements.** Eurostat (2021), *Applying the Degree of
Urbanisation: a methodological manual to define cities, towns and rural areas
for international comparisons*, Publications Office of the EU. Urban centre:
"Contiguous cells (without diagonals and with gap filling) with a density of
at least 1 500 inhabitants/km² and a minimum of 50 000 inhabitants". Urban
cluster: "Contiguous cells (including diagonals) with a density of at least
300 inhabitants/km² and a minimum of 5 000 inhabitants". Implemented here on
GHS-SMOD R2023A (Schiavina et al. 2023).

**Stochastic frontier models.** Aigner, D., Lovell, C. A. K. & Schmidt, P.
(1977), "Formulation and estimation of stochastic frontier production
function models", *Journal of Econometrics* 6(1), 21–37. Meeusen, W. & van
den Broeck, J. (1977), *International Economic Review* 18(2), 435–444. The
error is split into symmetric noise and a one-sided term, here "growth
since". The normal / half-normal form used here is the standard first
choice.

**Estimating each unit's one-sided term.** Jondrow, J., Lovell, C. A. K.,
Materov, I. S. & Schmidt, P. (1982), "On the estimation of technical
inefficiency in the stochastic frontier production function model",
*Journal of Econometrics* 19(2–3), 233–238.

**Ordinal regression.** McCullagh, P. (1980), "Regression models for
ordinal data", *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B* 42(2),
109–142. Used here only to show how a symmetric model misplaces the
boundaries.

**An alternative to the frontier model.** Quantile regression (Koenker, R. &
Bassett, G. (1978), "Regression quantiles", *Econometrica* 46(1), 33–50)
would fit a low quantile of density for each ring size. That is simpler,
but needs a quantile to be chosen by hand. The frontier model estimates the
split from the data.

**Classification trees.** Breiman, L., Friedman, J. H., Olshen, R. A. &
Stone, C. J. (1984), *Classification and Regression Trees*, Wadsworth.
Implemented in R by the `rpart` package, which ships with R. For trees whose
splits are chosen by significance tests rather than greedily: Hothorn, T.,
Hornik, K. & Zeileis, A. (2006), "Unbiased recursive partitioning: a
conditional inference framework", *Journal of Computational and Graphical
Statistics* 15(3), 651–674. For trees that split on how a model's
relationships change: Zeileis, A., Hothorn, T. & Hornik, K. (2008),
"Model-based recursive partitioning", *Journal of Computational and
Graphical Statistics* 17(2), 492–514. Both are in the R package `partykit`.

**Clusters.** Rousseeuw, P. J. (1987), "Silhouettes: a graphical aid to the
interpretation and validation of cluster analysis", *Journal of
Computational and Applied Mathematics* 20, 53–65.
